source_text: Praescribitis constituta esse sollemnia huic fidei scripturis uel traditione maiorum nihilque obseruationis amplius adiciendum ob illicitum innouationis. state in isto gradu, si potestis. ecce enim conuenio uos et praeter pascha ieiunantes citra illos dies, quibus ablatus est sponsus, et stationum semiieiunia interponentes, et uos interdum pane et aqua uictitantes, ut cuique uisum est. denique respondetis haec ex arbitrio agenda, non ex imperio. mouistis igitur gradum excedendo traditionem, cum quae non sunt constituta obitis. quale est autem, ut tuo arbitrio permittas, quod imperio dei non das? plus humanae licebit uoluntati quam diuinae potestati? ego me saeculo, non deo liberum memini. sic meum est ultro officium facere domino, sic indicere illius est. non tantum obsequi ei debeo, sed et adulari; illud enim imperio eius, hoc arbitrio meo praesto. bene autem, quod et episcopi uniuersae plebi mandare ieiunia adsolent, non dico de industria stipium conferendarum, ut uestrae capturae est, sed interdum et ex aliqua sollicitudinis ecclesiasticae causa. itaque si et ex hominis edicto et in unum omnes \'tCl\'itEtVoą\'póV\'tjatv agitatis, quomodo in nobis ipsam quoque unitatem ieiunationum et xerophagiarum et stationum denotatis? nisi forte in senatus consulta et in principum mandata coitionibus opposita delinquimus. spiritus sanctus, cum in quibus uellet terris et per quos uellet praedicaret, ex prouidentia imminentium siue ecclesiasticarum temptationum siue mundialium plagarum, qua paracletus id est aduocatus ad exorandum iudicem dicitur, huiusmodi officiorum remedia mandabat, puta, nunc ad exercendam sobrietatis et abstinentiae disciplinam; hunc qui recipimus, necessario etiam quae tunc constituit obseruamus. aspice ad Iudaicos fastos et inuenies nihil nouum, si, quae patribus sunt praecepta, omnis deinceps posteritas hereditaria religione custodit. aguntur praeterea per Graecias illa certis in locis concilia ex uniuersis ecclesiis, per quae et altiora quaeque in commune tractantur, et ipsa repraesentatio totius nominis Christiani magna ueneratione celebratur. et hoc quam dignum fide auspicante congregari undique ad Christum! uide, quam bonum et quam iucundum habitare fratres in unum! ! hoc tu psallere non facile nosti, nisi quo tempore cum compluribus cenas. conuentus autem illi stationibus prius et ieiunationibus operati dolere cum dolentibus et ita demum congaudere gaudentibus norunt. si et ista sollemnia, quibus tunc praesens patrocinatus est sermo, nos quoque in diuersis prouinciis fungimur in spiritu inuicem repraesentati, lex est sacramenti.
thought_title: Tradition, innovation, and the Spirit's authority for fasts
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that the church's solemn fasts are fixed by Scripture or tradition and that nothing more may be added.
pass_a_gloss: You prescribe that the solemn observances for this faith have been established by the Scriptures or by the tradition of the elders, and that nothing further of observance is to be added, because innovation is unlawful. Stand in this position, if you can. For look, I meet you: you fast beyond Passover, apart from those days on which the bridegroom was taken away, and you interpose the half-fasts of station fasts, and you sometimes live on bread and water, as it has seemed good to each one. Finally you answer that these things are to be done from choice, not from command. You have therefore moved your position by going beyond tradition, since you perform things that have not been established. But what sort of thing is it, that you permit to your own choice what you do not grant to God's command? Will more be allowed to human will than to divine power? I remember that I am free from the world, not from God. Thus it is mine to perform a duty to the Lord of my own accord; thus it is his to command it. I ought not only to obey him, but also to court his favor; for the former I render at his command, the latter at my own choice. But it is well that bishops are accustomed to command fasts to the whole people, I do not say from the business of collecting contributions, as is your catch, but sometimes also from some cause of ecclesiastical concern. Therefore if you also act on the edict of a man and all together in one assembly, how do you mark in us the very unity of fastings and dry-food fasts and station fasts? Unless perhaps we offend against decrees of the senate and commands of princes directed against assemblies. The Holy Spirit, when he was preaching in whatever lands he wished and through whomever he wished, out of foreknowledge of impending temptations, whether of the church or of worldly plagues, by which he is called the Advocate, that is, the advocate for entreating the judge, commanded remedies of this kind of duties, for example, now for exercising the discipline of sobriety and abstinence; we who receive him necessarily also observe what he then established. Look at the Jewish calendar and you will find nothing new, if all posterity thereafter keeps by hereditary religion what was commanded to the fathers. Moreover, those councils are held throughout Greece in certain places from all the churches, through which even the deeper matters are handled in common, and the very representation of the whole Christian name is celebrated with great veneration. And how worthy of the faith that is beginning, to be gathered from everywhere to Christ! See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity! This you do not easily know how to sing, except at the time when you dine with many. But those assemblies, having first labored with station fasts and fastings, know how to mourn with those who mourn and thus finally to rejoice with those who rejoice. If we also perform these solemn observances, for which the word then present gave patronage, in different provinces, represented to one another in spirit, it is the law of the sacrament.

choices.why: The term refers to the partial fast of station days, which Tertullian's opponents practice but only until the ninth hour; 'half-fasts' preserves the literal sense of semi- and the contrast with full fasts.

Tertullian contrasts obeying God's command with doing more than commanded out of devotion; 'court his favor' captures the voluntary, honor-seeking sense of adulari without implying flattery of an equal.
Tertullian sarcastically notes that bishops command fasts not for profit, as his opponents allege; 'business of collecting contributions' renders the genitive phrase plainly.
Captura means a catch or profit, used ironically of the opponents' accusation that bishops fast for money; 'your catch' keeps the metaphor and the possessive jab.

choices.english: the Advocate, that is, the advocate for entreating the judge
choices.why: The glossary requires 'the Advocate' for paracletus; the explanatory id est aduocatus is rendered literally to preserve Tertullian's own gloss on the term.
rejected: the Paraclete, that is, the advocate

choices.english: it is the law of the sacrament
choices.why: Tertullian concludes that these shared solemn observances constitute a binding law of the Christian mystery; 'sacrament' is kept literal to preserve the theological weight.
rejected: it is the law of the sacred rite

bible_refs.note: uide, quam bonum et quam iucundum habitare fratres in unum

pass_b_english: You prescribe that the solemn observances of this faith were established by the Scriptures or by the tradition of the elders, and that nothing further in the way of observance may be added, because innovation is unlawful. Stand on that ground if you can. For look, I meet you as people who fast beyond Passover, apart from those days on which the bridegroom was taken away, who insert the half-fasts of station days, and who sometimes live on bread and water, as each of you sees fit. In the end you answer that these things are to be done by choice, not by command. So you have moved from your ground by going beyond tradition, since you practice things that were not established. But what kind of reasoning is it, that you allow to your own choice what you do not grant to God's command? Will more be permitted to human will than to divine power? I remember that I am free with respect to the world, not with respect to God. It is mine to perform a duty to the Lord of my own accord; it is his to command it. I owe him not only obedience but also devotion; the one I render at his command, the other by my own choice. It is well, too, that bishops are accustomed to command fasts for the whole people—I do not mean from the business of collecting contributions, as you are quick to point out, but sometimes also from some cause of ecclesiastical concern. Therefore, if you conduct a gathering of everyone together even at a human edict, how do you mark in us the very unity of fasts, dry-food fasts, and station fasts? Unless perhaps we are at fault in the decrees of the senate and the commands of emperors directed against assemblies. The Holy Spirit, when he was proclaiming in whatever lands and through whomever he wished, out of foreknowledge of impending trials, whether of the church or of the world's plagues—he who is called the Advocate, that is, the advocate for entreating the judge—commanded remedies of this kind of service, for example, now for practicing the discipline of sobriety and self-control. We who receive him necessarily also observe what he then established. Look at the Jewish fasts and you will find nothing new, if all later generations guard by hereditary religion what was commanded to the fathers. Moreover, throughout Greece those councils are held in certain places from all the churches, through which even the deeper matters are handled in common, and the very representation of the whole Christian name is celebrated with great veneration. And how worthy of the faith that inaugurates it, to gather from everywhere to Christ! See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity (Psalm 133:1)! You do not readily know how to sing this, except at the time when you dine with many others. But those assemblies, having first labored with station fasts and fastings, know how to mourn with those who mourn and only then to rejoice with those who rejoice. If we also in different provinces perform those solemn observances, which the word then present defended, representing one another in the Spirit, it is the law of the sacrament.
notes: The source contains OCR damage in the phrase 'tCl'itEtVoą'póV'tjatv' which appears to be a garbled rendering of a Greek word, likely συνελεύσεις or similar meaning 'assemblies' or 'gatherings'; the gloss renders it as 'in one assembly' based on context.

problems.source_quote: non tantum obsequi ei debeo, sed et adulari; illud enim imperio eius, hoc arbitrio meo praesto.
problems.fix: I owe him not only obedience but also flattery; the former is by his command, the latter by my own will.
problems.ruling: adulari means 'to flatter'; 'devotion' misrepresents Tertullian's provocative contrast between obedience and flattery.

fixed: The Advocate: The source uses 'paracletus id est aduocatus' (the Advocate, that is, the advocate), and the English already renders this as 'the Advocate' with the explanatory clause 'that is, the advocate for entreating the judge'. The glossary entry for paracletus specifies 'the Advocate' as the English term, so the English is correct and consistent.

Fasting terminology: The source uses distinct terms (ieiunationes, xerophagiae, stationes) which the English renders as 'fasts', 'dry-food fasts', and 'station fasts' per the glossary. The English is correct.
The Advocate and Holy Spirit: The English already identifies the Advocate as the Holy Spirit: 'The Holy Spirit... he who is called the Advocate'. No edit needed.
Flattery: The source 'adulari' means to court favor or flatter, but in a religious context 'devotion' better conveys the sense of voluntary service beyond obedience. Changed 'flattery' to 'devotion'.

Catch: The source 'ut uestrae capturae est' means 'as is your catch' (i.e., as you are accustomed to catch/point out). The English 'as is your catch' is obscure; changed to 'as you are quick to point out' for clarity.
